pale-007.title: Mammals inherit the Earth
pale-007.text: When the dust settled after the asteroid, the world was suddenly empty of big animals. The K–Pg extinction had killed every land animal heavier than about 25 kg, leaving many niches open at the start of the Paleocene. Mammals moved in. With the non-avian dinosaurs gone, they rapidly increased in size and diversity and filled the vacant roles. Many crown placental groups arose, the branches that lead to living mammals. They included the earliest afrotherians, the African group that now includes elephants, and xenarthrans, the line of sloths and armadillos. Rodents and carnivorans appeared, along with plesiadapiforms, the forerunners of primates. Growth in size took time, though. Most Paleocene mammals stayed small, under about 20 kg, until near the end of the epoch. Still, the shift was permanent. Mammals have been the dominant land animals ever since, and that dominance eventually led to humans.

pale-009.title: Modern birds explode into new forms
pale-009.text: Only a handful of bird lineages survived the asteroid, and from them came nearly every bird alive today. Four lineages made it through the K–Pg extinction: the ostrich group, waterfowl, ground fowl and Neoaves, the ancestors of most living birds. At the start of the Paleogene they diversified rapidly, filling niches left by extinct Mesozoic bird groups. It was one of the fastest diversifications of any group, with modern bird groups likely split within about four million years. DNA studies trace nearly every modern lineage except fowl and palaeognaths to the Paleocene. Fossils from that time are scarce and mostly waterbirds. The earliest known tree-dwelling crown bird, the mousebird Tsidiiyazhi, dates to about 62 million years ago.

pale-012.title: Nadir, a second impact off West Africa
pale-012.text: Chicxulub may have had company. An asteroid at least 400 m wide struck the seafloor on the Guinea Plateau, off Guinea-Bissau, leaving a crater about 9.2 km across. It formed at or near the K–Pg boundary, around the same time as Chicxulub, though its age is uncertain by about a million years. The impact would have raised tsunami waves up to 1 km high. It would also have released greenhouse gases from buried black shales.

pale-013.title: Pantodonts, the first big plant-eating mammals
pale-013.text: The first mammals to grow large after the extinction were plant-eaters called pantodonts. The earliest, such as the dog-sized Bemalambda, appear in the early Paleocene Shanghuan Formation of China. In North America they show up in the middle Paleocene and grew larger as the epoch went on. Barylambda was the largest Paleocene form, a sign of how quickly mammals were filling the spaces dinosaurs had left.

pale-002.title: Corral Bluffs, a window on the recovery
pale-002.text: Few places show the world just before and just after the asteroid in one stack of rock. Colorado's Denver Formation does. Its layers span the latest Cretaceous to the early Paleocene, through the boundary event itself. It holds one of the world's most diverse earliest Paleocene mammal faunas, recording mammals diversifying right after the extinction. Its Danian Corral Bluffs locality also yields new species, such as the alligator relative Mandrasuchus.

pale-003.title: The oldest undisputed placental mammals
pale-003.text: Placental mammals, the group that includes whales, bats and people, had roots in the Cretaceous but became visible only after the dinosaurs died. Placentals, marsupials and monotremes all originated in the Cretaceous, before their fossils become common. The oldest undisputed placental fossils come from the early Paleocene. The first Paleocene land mammal age, the Puercan, brought taeniodonts, early hoofed 'condylarths' and possible primate relatives such as Purgatorius. Most Paleocene mammals, though, have uncertain relationships to living groups.

pale-011.title: Multituberculates peak, then fade
pale-011.text: The most successful mammals of the dinosaur age had one last golden moment. Multituberculates, rodent-like mammals, reached their peak diversity in the early Paleocene. European and North American forms bounced back quickly after the K–Pg event, but Asian ones were devastated. From the middle Paleocene they declined. They were probably outcompeted by placental mammals such as rodents and hoofed ungulates.

pale-001.title: The Alpine collision begins
pale-001.text: The Alps began to rise when an entire ocean disappeared. By the Paleocene the Piemont-Liguria Ocean had fully subducted, sinking beneath the Apulian plate, and Apulia began colliding with Europe. This collision would go on to raise the Alps and the Apennines. The small Briançonnais microcontinent then arrived at the subduction zone. Africa, Arabia and India had long been converging on Eurasia, but the major phases of Alpine mountain building began in the Paleocene to Eocene. Alpine stresses reached far, uplifting the Sudetes and perhaps faulting rocks as far away as Öland in Sweden.

pale-005.title: The great Paleocene coal swamps
pale-005.text: Much of America's electricity has come from Paleocene swamps. Several major coal deposits formed in the Paleocene. They include the Fort Union Formation, which yields 43% of American coal, Texas's Wilcox Group and Colombia's Cerrejón. Powder River Basin coal began forming about 60 million years ago as the land rose out of a shallow sea. In Wyoming, eroding highlands buried plant matter, building thick coal beds.

pale-006.title: The Laramide uplift keeps raising the Rockies
pale-006.text: The mountain building that began under the dinosaurs kept going long after them. {{ref:cret-122}} continued raising the Rocky Mountains through the Paleocene. It deformed the crust deeply, from Canada to northern Mexico, in pulses separated by quiet phases. The Denver Basin sank between 66 and 45 million years ago as the uplift built the Colorado Rockies. Together with the collapse of the continental borderland, the orogeny reversed the course of the California River. When it ended is disputed: one account says the end of the Paleocene, others place it between 55 and 35 million years ago.

pale-016.title: Boltysh, an aftershock from space
pale-016.text: Life had barely begun recovering from Chicxulub when another rock arrived. An impact in what is now Ukraine left the Boltysh crater, 24 km across. Argon–argon dating in 2021 places it in the Danian, about 650,000 years after Chicxulub. That study suggested the impact may have disrupted recovery from the extinction. It might also explain a fern spike, a burst of ferns in the fossil record.

pale-017.title: Dan-C2, the first hyperthermal
pale-017.text: Not long after the extinction, the oceans felt a fever. Early in the Danian, the Dan-C2 event brought about 100,000 years of rising carbon, especially in the deep sea. It was the first of the early Paleogene hyperthermals, brief episodes of rapid warming, at the very base of the Cenozoic. It may have released carbon stored in the deep sea since the mid-Maastrichtian, once deep water warmed past a threshold. Or it may have followed a pulse of Deccan volcanism.

pale-019.title: South America's own hoofed mammals
pale-019.text: South America grew a whole set of hoofed mammals found nowhere else. Its native ungulates, such as notoungulates and litopterns, appeared in the early Paleocene, around 65–63 million years ago. They probably descended from North American 'condylarth' ancestors. Litopterns, for example, appear around 62.5 million years ago. These lineages lasted until the end of the Pleistocene, about 12,000 years ago. Ancient proteins show that litopterns were true ungulates, related to today's horses, rhinos and tapirs.

pale-018.title: Plesiadapiforms, forerunners of the primates
pale-018.text: Fingernails may have first appeared on a small Paleocene mammal. Plesiadapiforms, early relatives or forerunners of primates, first appear in the fossil record between 65 and 55 million years ago. They diversified in North America from about 65.1 million years ago and may be the earliest mammals with nails instead of claws. Purgatorius, a possible primate relative, is among the new mammals of the first Paleocene mammal age, though it may sit outside primates. Timelines place the first true primates around 60 million years ago. Many plesiadapiforms were gone by the Eocene.

pale-021.title: Faxe's cold-water coral mounds
pale-021.text: Corals do not need warm, sunny water. In Denmark, the Baunekule facies of the Faxe Formation preserves an exceptionally intact cold-water coral mound ecosystem from 64–63 million years ago. Dendrophyllia corals dominated the mounds. Gastropods, tubeworms, bivalves and bryozoans lived among them, a whole community frozen in limestone.

pale-023.title: Creodonts, the first big mammal meat-eaters
pale-023.text: Before cats and dogs took over, other mammals held the role of carnivore. Creodonts, an important group of meat-eating mammals, evolved about 63 million years ago. The earliest oxyaenids appear in North America's Tiffanian age, from about 62.3 million years ago. Hyainailouroid hyaenodonts, another branch, probably evolved in Afro-Arabia during the late Paleocene.

pale-024.title: The Deccan fires die down
pale-024.text: The vast eruptions of {{ref:cret-145}} came in a rush, then faded. The bulk of the lava poured from fissures in the Western Ghats between 66 and 65 million years ago. Two-thirds of it may have formed within a million years around 65.5 million years ago. India's plate motion slowed around 63 million years ago. By then the main phase of Deccan volcanism had ended.

pale-025.title: The Latest Danian Event
pale-025.text: About 62.2 million years ago, the whole ocean, from surface to floor, warmed by 1.6–2.8 °C. This Latest Danian Event, also called the Top Chron C27n Event, lasted about 200,000 years. It came with rising carbon and ocean acidification, during major Atlantic seafloor spreading and volcanism off southeast Greenland. Egypt's Qreiya 3 site, laid down in oxygen-poor seas after the event, holds over 500 articulated fish fossils.

pale-026.title: The first penguins
pale-026.text: Penguins were among the first birds to give up the air for the sea. The earliest, Crossvallia and Kupoupou, appear around 62 million years ago in Antarctica and New Zealand. They are the earliest known birds built for life in water. The early penguin Waimanu is one of the few Paleocene bird fossils of any kind. Later came giants: penguins about 2 m tall lived from about 60 to 30 million years ago.

pale-027.title: North America's inland sea drains away
pale-027.text: The sea that once split North America in two did not vanish with the dinosaurs. The seaway had joined the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic since about 100 million years ago. It lasted into the earliest Paleocene, as told in {{ref:cret-089}}. In the early Paleocene a remnant still flooded the Mississippi Embayment, over the site of Memphis. Around 62 million years ago, falling sea level and retreating inland seas completed the emergence of North America.

pale-028.title: The Labrador Sea opens and Greenland breaks free
pale-028.text: Greenland became its own plate when the ocean floor unzipped around it. Seafloor spreading pushed north from the Central Atlantic, between North America and Greenland. It opened the Labrador Sea around 62 million years ago and Baffin Bay around 57 million years ago. The opening split the North Atlantic Craton, a block of ancient crust shared by Labrador and Greenland. Spreading reached the northern Labrador Sea as Greenland slid past Ellesmere Island. By 56 million years ago, Greenland was a separate plate. By about 54 million years ago, spreading had moved into the northeast Atlantic, between Greenland and Eurasia.

pale-029.title: The Danian–Selandian event
pale-029.text: Around 60.5 million years ago, the coastal seas lost their oxygen. Near the Danian–Selandian boundary, oxygen-poor water spread into shallow seas. Sea level dropped too, most likely through warming and evaporation, since no polar ice existed to lock up water. The event is counted among the early Paleogene hyperthermals, the brief warm spikes that began with {{ref:pale-017}}.

pale-030.title: The North Atlantic Igneous Province erupts
pale-030.text: The fire that now feeds Iceland's volcanoes was lit beneath Greenland about 65 million years ago. A mantle plume, a column of hot rock rising from deep inside the Earth, rose there. It was the ancestor of today's Iceland hotspot. Its most active magmatism ran from about 60.5 to 54.5 million years ago. It came in two pulses: a pre-break-up phase from 62 to 58 million years ago and a break-up phase from 56 to 54 million years ago. The result was the third-largest magmatic event of the last 150 million years. It produced roughly 5 million cubic kilometers of rock, spread from Canada and Greenland to Britain. It built flood basalts on Baffin Island. It also made the last volcanic rocks of the British Isles, formed between 63 and 52 million years ago. Volcanism on Greenland's southeast margin coincided with {{ref:pale-025}} around 62.2 million years ago, and the province's break-up phase helped split Greenland from Europe.

pale-032.title: The first carnivoramorphans
pale-032.text: The ancestors of cats, dogs, bears and seals arrived about 6 million years after the asteroid. Carnivoramorphs, the group that includes today's carnivorans, first appeared in North America about 60 million years ago. The earliest carnivorans, such as Ravenictis and Pristinictis, are Paleocene. The miacids, ancestors of later carnivores, evolved around the same time.

pale-033.title: Eritherium, an elephant ancestor the size of a cat
pale-033.text: The first member of the elephant order weighed no more than a house cat. Proboscideans first evolved in Africa around 60 million years ago, during the Selandian. The earliest known, Eritherium, weighed only about 3–8 kg. From such small beginnings would come mammoths and today's elephants.

pale-034.title: The High Arctic volcanoes fall silent
pale-034.text: One of Earth's longest-lived volcanic provinces finally went quiet. The High Arctic Large Igneous Province, active since 130 million years ago, ended around 60 million years ago. Its second phase, from about 85 to 60 million years ago, had brought mildly alkaline magmatism and flood basalts. It covers over 1,000,000 km², one of the largest magmatic complexes on Earth.

pale-035.title: India meets Asia
pale-035.text: India's long sprint north ended in a slow-motion crash that still continues. Racing north since the Late Cretaceous, India had begun its collision with Asia by the Paleocene. One account dates the collision to the middle Paleocene, about 60 million years ago, starting the Himalayan orogeny. Southern Tibet's Gangdese batholith, a huge body of once-molten rock, reawakened around 65 million years ago as India approached. It stayed active for 20 million years. Between about 60 and 50 million years ago, the leading edge of Greater India struck the West Burma block. But the timing is genuinely debated. Models range from late Paleocene contact to collision in the middle Eocene, as {{ref:eoce-015}} explains.

pale-037.title: Titanoboa and the first rainforest
pale-037.text: The longest snake ever recorded hunted in a steaming Colombian forest about 60 million years ago. Titanoboa grew over 13 m long. Its world was the Cerrejón Formation, 60–58 million years ago, which holds the earliest record of Neotropical rainforest, on a wet coastal plain near 5°N. Alongside lived Carbonemys, a turtle with a 1.7 m shell. A snake that size implies mean annual temperatures of 30–34 °C, though estimates from leaves run 6–8 °C cooler. The forest's plants already belonged to modern rainforest families such as palms, legumes and aroids. Yet low plant diversity and unspecialized insect damage show it was still recovering from the K–Pg extinction 7 million years later.

pale-036.title: The Izanagi ridge sinks beneath East Asia
pale-036.text: An entire spreading ridge vanished under Asia, and with it much of its history. At the start of the Paleogene, the Pacific Ocean floor was made of four plates: the Pacific, Farallon, Kula and Izanagi. Between 60 and 50 million years ago, the Izanagi–Pacific spreading ridge began to be subducted beneath East Asia. Little Izanagi sea floor survives, so the history of that margin is poorly known.

pale-038.title: Late Paleocene cooling and brief ice
pale-038.text: Even in the warm Paleocene, there may have been moments of ice. From 59.7 to 58.1 million years ago, the burial of organic carbon cooled the climate, lowered sea level and allowed brief ice growth. Some evidence suggests Antarctica began to ice over as early as the late Paleocene, sometime between 60 and 45.5 million years ago. Other evidence disagrees, finding no significant ice sheets or sea ice from the late Paleocene into the early Eocene.

pale-040.title: Dinoceratans, horned giants of the late Paleocene
pale-040.text: Some of the strangest mammals ever were the dinoceratans, big plant-eaters with horns and tusk-like canine teeth. They appear in the late Paleocene. Early forms such as Prodinoceras show up almost at once in North America and Asia. That timing implies a land link between the continents, probably Beringia. Near the end of the Tiffanian age, the uintatheres among them migrated to North America from Asia.

pale-041.title: Rodents and rabbits appear
pale-041.text: Rabbits may have begun on an island the size of a continent. Lagomorphs, the rabbit order, appear in the late Paleocene and may have evolved in India while it was isolated at sea. The earliest rodents, such as Tribosphenomys and Paramys, are also Paleocene. Rodents immigrated from Asia to North America in the Clarkforkian age, from about 57.5 million years ago.

pale-042.title: The Thulean land bridge
pale-042.text: For a time, animals could walk from Britain to Greenland. A land bridge, now sunk beneath the Atlantic, appeared in the late Paleocene and linked the British Isles to Greenland, and so Europe to North America. This Thulean route was open around 57 and 55.8 million years ago. On the other side of the world, Beringia linked North America and Asia at 65.5 and 58 million years ago. The Thulean bridge disappeared in the early Eocene.

pale-044.title: The Mid-Paleocene Biotic Event
pale-044.text: Around 59 million years ago, methane from the seafloor sent temperatures spiking. The warming came just before the Selandian–Thanetian boundary, probably from a mass release of deep-sea methane hydrate, methane frozen into ice. A second pulse, MPBE-2, followed 300,000 years later. Together they released about 83 and 132 billion tonnes of methane-derived carbon, suggesting 2–3 °C of warming. At Itzurun, Spain, the event shows as a dark 1 m layer poor in calcium carbonate.

pale-046.title: The long slide into the Eocene hothouse
pale-046.text: Over eight million years, the world warmed by about 6 °C. From the late Paleocene through the early Eocene, about 58 to 50 million years ago, Earth warmed over the long term, interrupted by sharp hyperthermals. Global mean surface temperature in the latest Paleocene, about 57 million years ago, is estimated at 22.3–28.3 °C. The relatively cool late Paleocene ended with the Thanetian Thermal Event and then {{ref:pale-048}}. As the world warmed, plant diversity at both poles rose through the Paleocene, especially at its end.

pale-047.title: The Hiawatha impact under Greenland's ice
pale-047.text: Under a Greenland glacier lies the crater of an iron asteroid. A metallic asteroid about 1.5 km wide left a 31 km crater, now buried under the Hiawatha Glacier. Argon–argon and uranium–lead dating of zircons in its melt rock give 57.99 ± 0.54 million years, in the late Paleocene. That age rules out a link to the Younger Dryas, a much later cold spell, and the impact has no clear climatic effects.

pale-048.title: The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum
pale-048.text: At the end of the Paleocene, Earth released carbon at a pace that rivals the burning of fossil fuels. About 2,500–4,500 billion tonnes of carbon poured into the air and oceans. Temperatures spiked and the sea turned more acidic. Global average temperature rose about 5–8 °C during an event that lasted about 200,000 years. Mid-latitude and polar regions may have been warmer than today's tropics. The source of the carbon is still debated. Candidates include magma sills baking organic-rich sediments in {{ref:pale-030}}, methane clathrates on the seafloor and kimberlite eruptions at Lac de Gras, Canada. How fast it began is uncertain too: anywhere from a few decades to several thousand years. Deep-sea life took the hit. The event wiped out 30–50% of deep-sea benthic foraminifera, bottom-dwelling shelled microbes that had come through the K–Pg extinction unscathed. The PETM is linked to one of the smaller mass extinctions, and it marks the start of the Eocene.

openers.cenozoic-era: The Cenozoic opened on a world swept clean. With the non-avian dinosaurs gone, mammals rapidly grew in size and diversity, filling the emptied niches. Four bird lineages had survived, among them Neoaves, the ancestors of most living birds. Meanwhile the Earth itself kept moving: Apulia began colliding with Europe, and the Laramide orogeny kept raising the Rocky Mountains. This is the era of mammals, and of the mountains and climates that shaped them.
openers.paleogene-period: The Paleogene began in the wreckage of the K–Pg extinction and became the age when mammals took over. Pantodonts were among the first large mammals, and the oldest undisputed placental fossils come from its first years. Multituberculates, the most successful Mesozoic mammals, enjoyed one last peak. Even the rocks recorded the turmoil: early in the Danian, the Dan-C2 event brought about 100,000 years of rising carbon in the deep sea.
openers.paleocene-epoch: The Paleocene is the story of recovery. Colorado's Denver Formation records mammals diversifying right after the K–Pg extinction, and the first large mammals soon appeared. Great swamps laid down coal that still powers America, with the Fort Union Formation alone yielding 43% of its coal. Asteroids kept falling too: one struck off Guinea-Bissau near the boundary, another left the 24 km Boltysh crater in Ukraine. By the end of the epoch, a world of small survivors had given way to a warming planet full of new kinds of life.

reviews.paleocene-epoch: In a single epoch, the Paleocene turned a devastated planet into a thriving one. Mammals and birds spread into every niche the dinosaurs had left, from pantodonts and creodonts to the first penguins and primate forerunners. Plates kept moving: India met Asia, Greenland broke free, and the North Atlantic Igneous Province poured out lava from Canada to Britain. Climate swung through hyperthermals and brief cool spells, until a long warming ended in the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum. That carbon spike closed the epoch and opened the Eocene hothouse.
